newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians to go to polls amid more bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Algerians to go to polls amid more bloodshed.

text.p: Algerians head to the polls on Thursday to vote on constitutional changes banning Moslem militants from seeking power amid fresh evidence their country is still trapped in a ferocious cycle of violence.
Five people were killed and 15 wounded on Sunday when a car bomb exploded in the garrison town of Blida, south of the capital Algiers, Algerian security forces said in a statement.

The bombing followed a series of raids on villages and bomb attacks -- blamed by the authorities on Islamist rebels -- in which more than 120 people, including women and children, were massacred in the past six weeks.
Algerian newspapers have dubbed the month leading to the November 28 referendum the "Month of all horrors".
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which Islamists had taken a huge lead.

Officials have urged the country's 16.4 million eligible voters to turn en masse to the 35,533 polling offices to cast white "yes" ballots to endorse the constitution change they see as the way to civil peace.
But the most feared Islamic militant group, the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), warned voters not to go to polls, threatening to "strike the necks" of those who dare leave their homes on referendum day.

Most secular opposition groups -- saying the changes would lead to "institutional dictatorship" -- have called on supporters to cast black "no" ballots. Two legal Islamist groups have told supporters to vote "no" while a vocal anti-Islamist party called for a boycott.
Supporters of the changes, led by President Liamine Zeroual, argue that the constitutional reforms aim to strenghten the multi-party system.
They say the change will force politicians to focus on acute social and economic problems instead of squabbling over the country's culture, like Moslem religion and Arab language.
They also stress the reforms are unavoidable to break with the past decade which they say was marked by weak leadership and murky relations between the regime's various "centres of power".

"This revised constitution is a response to the serious problems Algeria went through under the shelter of democracy," Agriculture Minister Nouredine Bahbouh told a campaign meeting in the western town of Saida last week.
"It will put an end to confusion spawned by the 1989 constitution which allowed some politicians to damage the nation's interests."

The draft constitution broadens the president's paramount powers but it limits him to two five-year terms. It guarantees for the first time since independence from France in 1962 the right to form opposition parties to compete for government.
But it bans the use of Islam, Arab and Berber languages, gender and regional differences as means to seek power.

Anti-Islamist leader Said Saadi, saying the changes were a "declaration of war against democracy", urged voters to stay away from the polls. He warned them that "the authorities' election machine will mill your votes into 'yes' ballots".
But the government promised the vote would be fair.

"I assert that the government has made and will make its utmost to enable Algeria's citizens once again to excercise their right to vote in full freedom and tranquillity," said Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour.
The GIA, which wants to topple Zeroual and install a purist Islamic government, warned voters to stay at home on referendum day.
"We will strike with force the neck of anyone who goes to vote," the GIA said in a statement last week.
The security forces deployed thousands of troops across the country over the weekend, increasing the number of roadblocks and patrols in and around main cities to prevent any attacks.
